narration.text: This lesson covers what California's DUI law includes. Many drivers think of DUI as only about alcohol, but the law covers alcohol and every impairing drug alike, including medicines from a doctor or pharmacy. We will look at the situations in which driving becomes illegal, what refusing a test costs, how the law reaches young people who ride bicycles under the influence, and the rules for alcohol and cannabis inside a vehicle, including where open containers may be carried. Knowing the full scope helps you avoid breaking the law without meaning to.

lines.text: No line between street drugs and medicines.
Tolerance falls with age.

narration.text: California DUI law covers alcohol and every impairing drug alike. It draws no line between street drugs and medicines from a doctor or pharmacy. If a substance impairs your driving, the law applies. Alcohol tolerance also falls as drivers age, so an amount that once seemed fine may affect an older driver more. The key idea is that the law looks at impairment, not at whether the substance was legal to buy or prescribed to you. A prescription bottle does not make it legal to drive while impaired by what is inside it.

lines.text: Excessive alcohol in any form.
Any impairing drug, or a mix.
Refusing a test costs a year.

narration.text: Driving is illegal after excessive alcohol in any form, including cough syrup, after any impairing drug, including prescriptions and over-the-counter pills, or after any impairing mix of alcohol and drugs. Read every label on the medicines you take. And know that refusing a chemical test costs a year of driving. So the illegal-after triggers cover alcohol, drugs, and mixes of the two. A small amount of alcohol combined with a medicine can impair you more than either alone, which is why the mix is listed as its own trigger.

lines.text: Riders thirteen to twenty: bike DUI counts.
No drinking or cannabis while driving or riding.
Open containers in the trunk.

narration.text: Riders aged thirteen to twenty who are convicted of bicycling under the influence face a one-year suspension of their license, or a one-year delay in getting one once they are eligible to drive. Nobody may drink alcohol or use cannabis while driving or riding in a vehicle. Containers you carry must stay sealed and unopened, and opened ones ride in the trunk or another non-passenger area, never the glove box. Passengers in buses, taxis, campers, and motorhomes are exempt from the container rule. So container law pairs sealed carrying with trunk-only open storage.

Open containers must ride in the trunk or a non-passenger area, never the glove box. A third trap is thinking a bicycle is outside the law; riders thirteen to twenty convicted of bicycling under the influence can lose a year of driving.

Passengers in buses, taxis, campers, and motorhomes are exempt. If you answered no, you have the container rule. If you answered yes, remember that the glove box sits within reach of the driver and passengers, which is exactly why the handbook rules it out for open containers.

Driving is illegal after excessive alcohol in any form, any impairing drug, or any impairing mix, so read every label, and refusing a test costs a year of driving. Riders aged thirteen to twenty convicted of bicycling under the influence face a one-year suspension or licensing delay. No one may drink or use cannabis in a vehicle, and open containers ride in the trunk or a non-passenger area.

narration.text: This lesson covers blood alcohol concentration, or BAC, and what happens after a DUI stop. The legal BAC limit is not the same for every driver; it depends on your age, whether you are on DUI probation, and what kind of license you hold. We will look at each limit, how BAC tables estimate your level and what counts as one drink, the rule that extends the ban to boats and jet skis, what you agree to by driving in California, what happens at a DUI arrest, and the long list of penalties that a DUI conviction can bring.

lines.text: Over twenty-one: zero point zero eight percent.
Under twenty-one or DUI probation: zero point zero one.
Commercial and paid hauling: zero point zero four.

narration.text: Illegal BAC starts at zero point zero eight percent for drivers over twenty-one, zero point zero one percent for drivers under twenty-one, zero point zero one percent at any age for drivers on DUI probation, and zero point zero four percent for commercial licenses and drivers hauling paying passengers. Driving below these limits can still be unsafe, and a DUI conviction needs no BAC reading at all. So the limits step down by age, probation, and license class, and impairment can be convicted below every one of those lines. Know which line applies to you before you ever drink and drive.

lines.text: Tables use drinks, gender and weight.
Subtract zero point zero one per forty minutes.
One drink can impair.

narration.text: BAC tables estimate your level from the number of drinks, your gender, and your weight, subtracting zero point zero one percent for every forty minutes without a drink. One drink means one and a half ounces of eighty-proof liquor, twelve ounces of five percent beer, or five ounces of twelve percent wine. Fewer than five in one hundred people exceed what the table shows, and even a single drink can impair. Alcohol and drugs are also illegal aboard boats, jet skis, water skis, and similar vessels under the Harbors and Navigation Code, so the ban extends onto the water.

lines.text: Drivers consent to breath, blood or urine tests.
Refusal suspends or revokes.
Arrest: thirty-day temporary license.

narration.text: By driving in California, you consent to breath, blood, or urine testing when you are suspected of DUI. A preliminary breath test does not excuse a blood test for drugs. Refusing suspends or revokes your driving. A DUI arrest triggers an Admin Per Se suspension: your license is seized and swapped for a thirty-day temporary license, and you may request a hearing within ten days of the arrest. So implied consent covers breath, blood, and urine, refusal ends your driving, and arrest pairs the suspension with the thirty-day temporary license and the ten-day hearing window.

lines.text: A year of lost driving and a DUI program.
Insurance proof, fees, possible interlock.
Jail, fines, impound, ten years on record.

narration.text: A DUI conviction suspends or revokes your driving for a year and adds a DUI program, proof of insurance with an SR twenty-two or SR one-P form, reissue fees, and possibly an ignition interlock device. On top of that come up to six months of jail, fines, impound and storage bills, and civil lawsuits for any injury or death. Convictions stay on your record for ten years, and repeat offenses bring harsher penalties. So convictions stack year-long loss of driving, programs, insurance proof, fees, interlocks, jail, fines, impounds, lawsuits, and a decade on your record.

lines.text: Trap: below the limit, no DUI.
Truth: impairment is convictable.

narration.text: Here is a trap. Drivers who know the zero point zero eight percent limit sometimes believe that staying just under it protects them. The handbook says driving below the limit can still be unsafe, and DUI convictions need no BAC reading at all. A second trap is thinking a breath test clears you of drug testing; a preliminary breath test never excuses drug bloodwork. A third trap is letting the hearing window pass. After a DUI arrest, a hearing must be requested within ten days, while the temporary license lasts thirty days.

lines.text: On DUI probation.
What is the BAC limit?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: what is the illegal BAC level for a driver on DUI probation, at any age? Choose your answer. The answer is zero point zero one percent. Drivers on DUI probation share that limit with drivers under twenty-one. Adults over twenty-one who are not on probation have the zero point zero eight percent limit, and commercial license holders and paid passenger haulers have zero point zero four percent. If you answered zero point zero one, you have the probation rule. Remember too that a conviction is possible below any of these limits.

lines.text: The BAC limit depends on who you are.
Arrest and conviction carry long penalties.

narration.text: To sum up, illegal BAC starts at zero point zero eight percent over twenty-one, zero point zero one percent under twenty-one or on DUI probation, and zero point zero four percent for commercial licenses and paid passenger hauling, and DUI convictions need no BAC reading. BAC tables subtract zero point zero one percent per forty drink-free minutes, and one drink can impair. The ban extends to vessels. Drivers consent to testing, refusal costs driving, and arrest brings a thirty-day temporary license with a ten-day hearing window. Convictions bring a year-long loss, programs, insurance proof, and ten years on record.

narration.text: This lesson covers the alcohol rules that apply only to drivers under twenty-one. These drivers face stricter limits on carrying alcohol, specific penalties if they are caught, and their own testing rules and BAC lines. We will look at when an under-twenty-one driver may have alcohol in the car at all, what happens if they are caught with it, what tests an officer may demand, and the two BAC lines that matter most for young drivers. The stakes are high: several of these rules can cost a year of driving or delay getting a license.

lines.text: A companion twenty-one or older is required.
Full containers sealed; opened ones in the trunk.
Exception: off-site liquor workers.

narration.text: Drivers under twenty-one may not carry alcohol unless a companion aged twenty-one or older is with them. Even then, full containers must stay sealed and unopened, and opened ones must ride in the trunk or a non-passenger area. There is one exception: drivers who work for an off-site liquor licensee may carry closed containers for that work. So the possession rule pairs the adult-companion requirement with sealed-container and trunk-storage rules, with the liquor-work exception as the only way around the companion requirement.

lines.text: Impound up to thirty days, fines, suspension.
PAS at zero point zero five or higher: more tests.
Conviction at zero point zero one: possible revocation.

narration.text: An under-twenty-one driver caught with alcohol may face an impound of up to thirty days, possible court fines, and a one-year suspension, or a licensing delay of up to one year if not yet licensed. Officers who suspect drinking may demand a handheld, PAS, or chemical test. A DUI conviction at zero point zero one percent or higher may revoke driving for a year and adds a licensed DUI program. A PAS reading of zero point zero five percent or higher may lead to an officer requiring a breath or blood test, and a later reading at that level may lead to arrest and suspension. These are the zero-one revocation line and the zero-five arrest line.

lines.text: Trap: sealed alcohol is always allowed.
Truth: a companion twenty-one or older is needed.

narration.text: Here is a trap. Many young drivers think that as long as a bottle is sealed, carrying it is fine. For drivers under twenty-one, that is not the rule. They carry no alcohol without a companion twenty-one or older, and even then full containers stay sealed and opened ones ride in the trunk. The only other exception is work for an off-site liquor licensee with closed containers. A second trap is mixing up the two BAC lines: zero point zero one percent is the conviction and revocation line, and zero point zero five percent is the PAS line that may lead to further testing and possible arrest.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: for a driver under twenty-one, which PAS reading may lead to an officer requiring a breath or blood test? Make your choice. The answer is zero point zero five percent or higher, and a later reading at that level may lead to arrest and suspension. The separate zero point zero one percent line applies to DUI convictions, which may revoke driving for a year and add a licensed DUI program. If you answered zero point zero five, you have the testing line. Keep the two numbers apart: zero-one for conviction and revocation, zero-five for testing and arrest.

lines.text: No alcohol without a companion.
Zero-one and zero-five lines.

narration.text: To finish this section, drivers under twenty-one may not carry alcohol without a companion aged twenty-one or older, with full containers sealed and opened ones in the trunk, except workers for off-site liquor licensees carrying closed containers. Getting caught may bring an impound of up to thirty days; the court may impose fines and a one-year suspension, or request a first-license delay of up to one year. Officers may demand handheld, PAS, or chemical tests. A DUI conviction at zero point zero one percent or higher may revoke driving for a year, and a PAS reading of zero point zero five percent or higher may lead to further testing and can mean arrest.
